William Ewart Gladstone. The dominant Liberal statesman of the Victorian era and a moralist in politics, championing free trade, electoral reform, and Irish autonomy.

Gladstone began his career as a high Tory and moved steadily toward radical Liberalism, emerging as a champion of electoral reform, Irish tenant rights, and free trade. He served as Prime Minister four times across 1868 to 1874, 1880 to 1885, 1886, and 1892 to 1894, giving him the second-longest tenure in British history behind only the combined service of Asquith and Campbell-Bannerman.

Gladstone reformed education, expanded the franchise repeatedly, and championed the secret ballot, transforming the electorate and making Britain more democratic. He articulated a moral theology of politics, seeing government as an instrument of conscience and justice rather than mere interest. This vision alienated many traditional Conservatives who saw politics as the management of power rather than the pursuit of principle.

Irish Home Rule became the centerpiece of his final decades in power. He pushed through three Home Rule bills in 1886, 1893, and 1895 that split both his party and the nation over Irish independence. These efforts consumed his later years and defined his legacy as much as his earlier reform work. He retired from Parliament at eighty-nine after his final term, having reshaped the boundaries of Liberal political philosophy and challenged the foundations of Conservative thought.
